definition: A microorganism that causes disease, such as a bacterium, virus, fungus or protist.
A single-celled prokaryotic microorganism. Some cause disease by releasing toxins into the body.
A non-living pathogen that invades host cells and uses them to replicate, damaging or destroying the cells.
A type of organism that can cause disease, such as rose black spot in plants or athlete's foot in humans.
A single-celled organism, some of which are pathogens — for example, the protist that causes malaria.
A disease caused by a pathogen that can be passed from one organism to another.
The passing of a pathogen from one organism to another, e.g. by air, water, direct contact or vectors.
An organism that carries and transmits a pathogen to another organism without being affected itself — e.g. the Anopheles mosquito transmits malaria.
A viral disease spread by droplets from sneezes and coughs, causing fever and a red skin rash. Can be fatal.
A virus spread by sexual contact or exchange of blood that attacks the immune system, eventually leading to AIDS.
A condition caused by HIV where the immune system is so damaged it can no longer fight off other infections.
Tobacco mosaic virus — a plant disease that causes a mosaic pattern of discolouration on leaves, reducing photosynthesis.
A bacterial disease spread through contaminated food that causes fever, abdominal cramps and vomiting.
A sexually transmitted bacterial disease causing pain when urinating and yellow/green discharge. Treated with antibiotics.
A fungal disease of plants causing black spots on leaves, which turn yellow and drop off, reducing photosynthesis.
A disease caused by a protist, transmitted by the Anopheles mosquito. Causes recurring fever and can be fatal.
The body's first line of defence against pathogens — acts as a physical barrier preventing entry.
A sticky substance produced in the nose and trachea that traps pathogens before they reach the lungs.
Tiny hairs in the trachea that beat to move mucus and trapped pathogens away from the lungs.
Produced in the stomach to kill pathogens in food and drink before they can cause infection.
A type of white blood cell that engulfs and digests pathogens in a process called phagocytosis.
The process by which phagocytes engulf and destroy pathogens.
A type of white blood cell that produces antibodies in response to a specific antigen.
A protein produced by lymphocytes that binds specifically to an antigen on a pathogen, leading to its destruction.
A unique protein on the surface of a pathogen that triggers an immune response.
A long-lived lymphocyte that remains after an infection and allows a faster immune response if the same pathogen is encountered again.
The introduction of a small amount of dead or weakened pathogen (or its antigens) into the body to stimulate an immune response without causing disease.
When enough people in a population are vaccinated that pathogens cannot spread easily, protecting unvaccinated individuals too.
A drug that kills or inhibits the growth of bacteria. Antibiotics do not work against viruses.
When bacteria evolve so that antibiotics are no longer effective against them, due to natural selection of resistant strains.
A drug that relieves symptoms such as pain and fever, but does not kill the pathogen.
A drug used to treat viral infections by inhibiting the development of viruses inside host cells.
A trial in which a new drug is tested on human volunteers to determine its safety and efficacy.
A dummy treatment that contains no active drug, used as a control in clinical trials to compare against the real treatment.
A clinical trial in which neither the patients nor the doctors know who is receiving the real drug or the placebo, to prevent bias.
A drug derived from foxglove plants used to treat heart conditions — an example of a plant-derived medicine.
The first antibiotic discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928 from the Penicillium mould.
An antibody produced from a single clone of cells, designed to target one specific antigen.
